rubric.name: Uses the article
rubric.description: Answers from what the article actually reports (the threats, the scam, the fake network), not from general knowledge.

rubric.name: Explains the AI angle
rubric.description: Explains concretely how AI or automation made the attack bigger, faster or more convincing.

rubric.name: Names an AI defence
rubric.description: Proposes a specific way AI can detect or prevent the threat, not just "use AI".

rubric.name: Weighs both sides
rubric.description: On the ethical questions, states a position AND the strongest argument against it.

rubric.name: Connects to the frameworks
rubric.description: Ties the argument to accountability, transparency, privacy, bias, or the laws in Topic 6 (GDPR, CCPA, the EU AI Act).

rubric.name: Discusses, does not expose
rubric.description: Discusses real incidents and public figures as reported, without adding personal data about private people.

outcome_logic.focus: You argued one side of the ethical questions. Every one of them has a real cost either way: a human in the loop is slower, full autonomy has no one to answer for mistakes. Name the strongest argument against your position before you settle on it.

You answered from general knowledge rather than from the article. The incident questions ask what happened in Romania: the threats that grew, the figure used in the deepfake, the fake network. Go back to the article and quote the detail.

You explained how AI helps the attacker but not how it defends. For each incident, name the AI tool on the defender’s side: deepfake detection, anomaly detection on accounts, threat intelligence that links a fake network.

You did not say who answers when the AI gets it wrong. Accountability is the question behind half of Topic 6: the vendor, the company that deployed it, or the analyst who trusted it. Pick one and say why.

You did not connect your answers to the laws in Topic 6. Monitoring employees and analysing personal data are exactly what GDPR, CCPA and the EU AI Act regulate; one sentence tying your position to them makes it defensible.

You accepted monitoring in the name of security without asking what it costs. Transparency, data minimisation and a clear limit on what is analysed are what keep a security tool from becoming surveillance.
Topic 7 turns the lens on the AI itself: prompt injection, where an attacker talks a model into breaking its own rules. The accountability question you argued here comes straight back.

tasks.instr: Article 1: “Cyberfraud in Romania up over 40pct in 2024, malware attacks up 286.8pct”
What types of cyber threats increased the most in 2024 in Romania?
tasks.answer: The threats that grew the most, from the article.

tasks.instr: How does automation or AI make these attacks more dangerous?
tasks.answer: How AI or automation makes them worse.

tasks.instr: What role could AI play in defending against these threats?
tasks.answer: The defensive role AI could play.

tasks.instr: Article 2: “National Bank of Romania Warns Consumers About Deepfake Videos”
What was the attack performed?
tasks.answer: The attack, in a sentence or two.

tasks.instr: In what way was the figure misused in the scam?
tasks.answer: How the public figure was misused.

tasks.instr: How could AI be used to help identify or prevent deepfake scams?
tasks.answer: How AI could spot or stop it.

tasks.instr: Article 3: “Meta Busts Fake Influence Ops in Romania, Azerbaijan & Taiwan”
What was the goal of the fake accounts on social media?
tasks.answer: The goal of the fake accounts.

tasks.instr: How might AI have been used to make the posts look real?
tasks.answer: How AI could have made them convincing.

tasks.instr: How can platforms use AI to detect fake networks?
tasks.answer: How platforms could detect them with AI.

tasks.instr: General question: Who should be held accountable if an AI system makes a wrong security decision (e.g., blocking legitimate users or missing a real threat)?
tasks.answer: Your group’s position, and the strongest argument against it.

tasks.instr: General question: Should AI systems in cybersecurity be allowed to make autonomous decisions, or must humans always remain “in the loop”?
tasks.answer: Your group’s position, and where you draw the line.

tasks.instr: General question: How transparent should companies be when they use AI to monitor employees or customers for security purposes?
General question: To what extent is it ethical for AI to analyze personal data (emails, chats, browsing habits) in the name of security?
tasks.answer: Your group’s position, and the limit you would set.

tasks.instr: General question: How can organizations ensure that AI-driven security tools don’t become tools for mass surveillance?
tasks.answer: The safeguards you would put in place.

tasks.instr: General question: Could AI in cybersecurity unfairly target certain groups or geographies due to biased training data?
tasks.answer: Your group’s view, with an example.

tasks.instr: General question: Is it ethical for governments or organizations to use AI offensively (e.g., in hacking back, cyber warfare, or automated penetration testing)?
tasks.answer: Your group’s position, and the strongest argument against it.

tasks.instr: General question: How can security professionals balance trust in AI tools with their own expertise?
tasks.answer: How you would strike the balance.

tasks.instr: General question: Should users be informed when AI, rather than a human, is responsible for detecting and responding to threats on their systems?
